exercises.prompt:
What does this script print?

```fsharp
type OptionBuilder() =
    member _.Bind(o, f) = Option.bind f o
    member _.Return x = Some x

let maybe = OptionBuilder()

let add a b =
    maybe {
        let! x = a
        let! y = b
        return x + y
    }

printfn "%A %A" (add (Some 2) (Some 3)) (add (Some 2) None)
```

feedback.message: Not yet — when `b` is `None`, the second `let!` calls `Option.bind` on `None`. What does that return?

hints: `Option.bind` on `None` returns `None` without calling the rest.
exercises.solution: With two `Some` values, both binds succeed and `return` wraps 5: `Some 5`. In the second call, `let! y = b` binds on `None`, which short-circuits the rest of the block: `None`. Output: `Some 5 None`.

exercises.prompt:
What is the **first** line printed by this script?

```fsharp
let mutable log = []
let a = async { log <- "async" :: log }
let t = task { log <- "task" :: log }
printfn "%A" (List.rev log)
Async.RunSynchronously a
printfn "%A" (List.rev log)
```

feedback.message: Not yet — one of the two blocks starts running as soon as it is created. Which one?
Not yet — an `async` block is a recipe; does anything start it before the first print?

hints: An `async { }` does nothing until it is started, here by `Async.RunSynchronously`.
exercises.solution: Creating `t` runs the task's body at once, adding `"task"`. Creating `a` only builds a recipe. So the first line is `["task"]`. After `Async.RunSynchronously a` runs the workflow, the second line is `["task"; "async"]`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this script print?

```fsharp
let xs =
    seq {
        yield 1
        yield! [ 2; 3 ]
        for i in 10..10..30 do
            yield i
    }
printfn "%d %d" (Seq.length xs) (Seq.sum xs)
```

feedback.message: Not yet — `yield!` yields every element of the list, not the list as one element.

hints: `yield!` splices in all the elements of another sequence.
exercises.solution: The sequence is 1, 2, 3, 10, 20, 30: six elements whose sum is 66. Output: `6 66`.

exercises.prompt: An F# library contains `module Pricing` with `let discount rate price = price * (1m - rate)`. How do C# developers call it?

options.label: `Pricing.discount(0.1m, 200m)`, a static method with two parameters
options.feedback: Yes. A module compiles to a static class, and a curried function with all its parameters becomes an ordinary static method.

options.label: `Pricing.discount(0.1m)(200m)`, calling it one argument at a time
options.feedback: Not yet — the compiler emits a normal two-parameter method for C#, not a chain of functions.

options.label: They cannot: F# modules are invisible to C#
options.feedback: Not yet — modules are ordinary static classes in the compiled assembly.

options.label: `new Pricing().discount(0.1m, 200m)`
options.feedback: Not yet — a module is static; there is nothing to instantiate.

hints: What does a module compile to?
Curried F# functions defined with all their parameters become methods with that many parameters.
exercises.solution: A module becomes a static class and its functions become static methods, so C# calls `Pricing.discount(0.1m, 200m)`. For a polished C# experience you might also give it a PascalCase name with the `CompiledName` attribute, following the component design guidelines.

exercises.prompt: How do you call `Int32.TryParse(string s, out int result)` idiomatically from F#?

options.label: `let ok, value = System.Int32.TryParse "42"`
options.feedback: Yes. F# turns the `out` parameter into a second element of a returned tuple.

options.label: `let mutable value = 0` then `System.Int32.TryParse("42", &value)`
options.feedback: Not yet — that also works (with a byref), but it is the C#-style way; the tuple form is idiomatic F#.

options.label: It cannot be called from F#, because F# has no `out` keyword
options.feedback: Not yet — F# handles `out` parameters automatically.

options.label: `System.Int32.TryParse "42" |> Option.ofObj`
options.feedback: Not yet — `Option.ofObj` converts nulls, and `TryParse` returns a tuple, not a possibly-null object.

hints: Look at how the lesson called `DateOnly.TryParseExact` and `TryGetValue`.
exercises.solution: Omit the `out` argument and F# returns it as part of a tuple: `let ok, value = Int32.TryParse "42"` gives `true` and `42`. Matching on it (`| true, n -> Some n | false, _ -> None`) is the usual way to turn a Try-method into an option.

exercises.prompt: In the lesson's `MailboxProcessor` example, a hundred deposits posted from parallel threads produced a balance of exactly 100. Why are no updates lost?

options.label: Only the agent's own loop touches the balance, and it processes one message at a time
options.feedback: Yes. Concurrency happens only in the queue; the state is owned by a single sequential loop.

options.label: `decimal` additions are atomic on all processors
options.feedback: Not yet — a `decimal` is 16 bytes, and its additions are not atomic. The agent's design, not the type, prevents the race.

options.label: `Array.Parallel.iter` actually runs the deposits one after another
options.feedback: Not yet — it really does post from several threads; it is the agent that serialises the work.

options.label: F# automatically puts a lock around every mutable variable
options.feedback: Not yet — F# adds no locks. The agent has no mutable variable at all: its state is a parameter of the recursive loop.

hints: Who can read or change the balance?
How many messages does the agent handle at the same time?
exercises.solution: The balance exists only as the parameter of the agent's recursive loop. Messages from any number of threads wait in the agent's queue, and the loop takes them one at a time, so there is never a moment when two updates interleave. This is the actor model's answer to shared mutable state.
